title: Git & GitHub
tagline: Version control and collaboration: the backbone of every engineering team.
overview:
Git records the history of your code so you can experiment safely, find when a bug was introduced, and collaborate without overwriting each other. GitHub adds pull requests, code review and CI.

You'll learn the everyday commit loop, branching and merging, syncing with remotes, rebasing your own branches cleanly, keeping secrets out of the repo, and resolving conflicts without fear.
objectives: Use the working tree / staging / commit model deliberately.
Branch, merge, and explain fast-forward vs merge commits.
Sync with GitHub using fetch, pull and push, and open pull requests.
Rebase personal branches safely and know when not to.
Write a correct .gitignore and resolve merge conflicts.
concepts: An immutable snapshot with a SHA ID.
A movable pointer to a commit.
Another copy of the repo, e.g. origin on GitHub.
Replaying commits on a new base.
Overlapping edits Git refuses to auto-merge.
notes: Commit early and often in small, coherent units.
`git status` and `git log --oneline --graph` are your map.
Secrets never go into Git. Use `.env` + .gitignore from day one.

explain: Why a pushed secret must be rotated
use: Interactive rebase to clean up commits
debug: Detached HEAD after checking out a commit
build: This app's repository with clean history and a CI-ready .gitignore

lessons.title: Git vs GitHub, repositories and the commit cycle
lessons.summary: init, clone, status, add, commit and log: the everyday loop.
lessons.simple: **Git** is a version-control tool on your computer that records snapshots of your project. **GitHub** is a website that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration (pull requests, issues, CI). You can use Git without GitHub; not the reverse.
lessons.technical:
A **repository** is your project plus a hidden `.git` directory holding its full history. Git tracks content through three areas:

1. **Working tree**: the files you edit.
2. **Staging area (index)**: what will go into the next commit. `git add` puts changes here.
3. **Repository**: committed snapshots. `git commit` records the staged snapshot with a message, author and parent.

Each commit has an ID (a SHA hash) and points to its parent(s), forming a history graph.

- `git init` turns the current directory into a repository. `git clone URL` copies an existing one, including history.
- `git status` shows modified, staged and untracked files. Run it constantly.
- `git add file` / `git add -p` (interactively choose hunks). `git diff` shows unstaged changes; `git diff --staged` shows what will be committed.
- `git commit -m "Add user signup endpoint"`. Messages: imperative mood, say what and why.
- `git log --oneline --graph` shows history compactly.

Commit small, coherent changes. A commit that mixes a bug fix, a refactor and formatting is hard to review and hard to revert.
lessons.analogy: Staging is packing a box before shipping: you choose exactly which items go in (`add`), then seal and label the box (`commit`). The warehouse shelf of sealed, labeled boxes is your history.

example.code:
$ git init demo && cd demo
$ echo "# Demo API" > README.md
$ git status --short
?? README.md
$ git add README.md
$ git commit -m "Add README"
[main (root-commit) 3f2a1c9] Add README
$ echo "print('hi')" > app.py
$ git add app.py && git commit -m "Add entry point"
$ git log --oneline
8d41e07 Add entry point
3f2a1c9 Add README
example.explain: `??` means untracked. Each commit is a snapshot with its own hash; the log shows newest first.

terms: Files as they are on disk now.
The snapshot being prepared for the next commit.
Immutable snapshot with message, author, parent and SHA ID.
A file Git has never been told to track.
mistakes: `git add .` blindly, committing secrets or build output.
Giant commits with messages like 'fix stuff'.
interview: What is the staging area for?
What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

lessons.title: Branches and merging
lessons.summary: Create branches, switch between them and merge work back.
lessons.simple: A **branch** is a movable label pointing at a commit. You create a branch to work on a feature without disturbing `main`, then **merge** it back when it's done.
lessons.technical:
Branches are cheap: just a pointer. `HEAD` points to the branch you're on. When you commit, the current branch's pointer moves forward.

- `git switch -c feature/login` creates and switches (older: `git checkout -b`).
- `git branch` lists branches; `git switch main` changes back.
- `git merge feature/login` (while on main) integrates the branch.

Two kinds of merge:
- **Fast-forward**: main hasn't moved since you branched, so Git just moves the main pointer forward. No new commit.
- **Three-way merge**: both branches have new commits. Git finds the common ancestor and creates a **merge commit** with two parents.

Typical team flow: short-lived feature branches off `main`, opened as pull requests, merged after review and CI. Delete merged branches: `git branch -d feature/login`.
lessons.analogy: Branches are bookmarks in a choose-your-own-adventure book. Moving a bookmark is free; merging is writing a chapter that joins two storylines.

example.code:
$ git switch -c feature/health
$ echo "def health(): return 'ok'" >> app.py
$ git commit -am "Add health check"
$ git switch main
$ git merge feature/health
Updating 8d41e07..b12c3d4
Fast-forward
 app.py | 1 +
$ git branch -d feature/health
example.explain: main had no new commits, so the merge was a fast-forward: no merge commit was needed.

terms: A named pointer to a commit.
Pointer to what you have checked out, usually a branch.
Merge that just moves the pointer forward.
A commit with two parents joining histories.
remember: Branches are cheap pointers; use one per feature or fix.
Fast-forward = no merge commit; diverged = merge commit.
Keep branches short-lived to avoid painful merges.
mistakes: Long-lived branches that drift for weeks.
Switching branches with uncommitted changes and getting confused (commit or `git stash` first).
interview: When does Git create a merge commit?
practice: Can you use: create a branch, commit twice, and merge with a merge commit?
Can you explain: why branches cost almost nothing in Git.

lessons.title: Remotes: push, pull, fetch and pull requests
lessons.summary: Synchronize with GitHub and collaborate through pull requests.
lessons.simple: A **remote** is another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub, named `origin`. You **push** your commits up, and **fetch/pull** others' commits down.
lessons.technical:
- `git remote -v` lists remotes. `git remote add origin git@github.com:you/api.git` adds one.
- `git push -u origin feature/login` uploads a branch and sets its upstream so later `git push` needs no arguments.
- `git fetch` downloads new commits into **remote-tracking branches** (`origin/main`) **without** changing your files.
- `git pull` = `git fetch` + integrate (merge, or rebase with `--rebase`) into your current branch.

Fetch is always safe; pull changes your working branch. `git log main..origin/main` shows what's new upstream before you pull.

A **pull request (PR)** is a GitHub feature, not a Git command: you push a branch and ask for it to be merged into `main`. The PR shows the diff, runs CI checks, and collects review comments. Good PRs are small, explain *why*, and pass tests.

`git push` is rejected if the remote has commits you don't have. Fix it by pulling first. Never use `git push --force` on shared branches; if you must rewrite your own branch, use `--force-with-lease`, which refuses if someone else pushed.
lessons.analogy: `fetch` is checking your mailbox and reading the letters. `pull` is reading them and immediately rearranging your desk according to what they say.

example.code:
$ git fetch origin
$ git log --oneline main..origin/main
a91f0e2 Fix pagination bug
$ git pull --rebase origin main
$ git push -u origin feature/login
remote: Create a pull request for 'feature/login' on GitHub by visiting:
remote:   https://github.com/you/api/pull/new/feature/login
example.explain: Inspect upstream first with fetch + log, then integrate. After pushing, GitHub suggests opening a PR.

terms: A named reference to another repository, e.g. origin.
The remote branch your local branch pushes to/pulls from.
GitHub's request-review-merge workflow for a branch.
remember: fetch = download only; pull = fetch + merge/rebase.
interview: Why is your push rejected and how do you fix it?
practice: Can you use: push a branch and open a PR?
Can you debug: 'Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally'.

lessons.title: Rebase basics
lessons.summary: Replay commits onto a new base for a linear history, and know when not to.
lessons.simple: **Rebase** moves your branch's commits so they start from a newer commit, as if you had begun your work later. The result is a straight-line history instead of merge commits.
lessons.technical:
On `feature`, `git rebase main` takes each commit unique to `feature`, and re-applies it on top of `main`'s tip. The replayed commits get **new SHAs** — they are new commits with the same changes.

Merge vs rebase:
- **Merge** preserves exactly what happened, adding merge commits. Never rewrites history.
- **Rebase** gives a clean linear history but rewrites your branch's commits.

The golden rule: **don't rebase commits that others have already based work on** (e.g. shared `main`). Rebasing your own unpushed or personal feature branch is fine.

`git rebase -i HEAD~3` (interactive) lets you squash, reorder or reword your last three commits before opening a PR. If a conflict occurs during rebase: fix files, `git add`, `git rebase --continue` — or `git rebase --abort` to go back.
lessons.analogy: Merge is writing "meanwhile, in the other timeline…" into the story. Rebase is rewriting your chapter so it starts after the latest events, as if it always had.

example.code:
$ git switch feature/search
$ git rebase main
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/search.
$ git log --oneline --graph -4
* 7c0e2aa Add search endpoint     (new SHA)
* a91f0e2 Fix pagination bug      (main)
* 8d41e07 Add entry point
$ git push --force-with-lease      # branch was pushed before; history changed
example.explain: The feature commit now sits on top of main. Because its SHA changed, the remote branch needs a (safe) force push.

terms: Re-apply commits on top of another base.
No merge commits; one straight line.
Force-push that fails if the remote changed unexpectedly.
remember: `--abort` gets you out of a rebase gone wrong.
mistakes: Rebasing main or another shared branch.
interview: When would you choose rebase over merge?
Why does rebasing change commit hashes?
practice: Can you use: squash 3 messy commits into one with interactive rebase?
Can you explain: the golden rule of rebasing.

lessons.title: .gitignore and resolving conflicts
lessons.summary: Keep junk and secrets out of Git, and resolve merge conflicts calmly.
lessons.simple: `.gitignore` lists files Git should not track, like virtual environments, build output and `.env` secrets. A **conflict** happens when two branches changed the same lines; Git stops and asks you to decide.
lessons.technical:
`.gitignore` patterns: `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.venv/`, `.env`, `node_modules/`, `*.log`, `!keep.log` (negation). It only affects **untracked** files: if a file is already committed, ignoring it does nothing until you `git rm --cached file`.

If you committed a secret, removing it in a new commit is **not enough** — it's still in history. Rotate (revoke) the secret immediately, then optionally purge history with `git filter-repo`.

Conflicts: Git marks the file:
```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout = 30
=======
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> feature/slow-api
```
Steps: `git status` (shows "both modified") → edit the file to the correct final content and delete the markers → run tests → `git add file` → `git commit` (merge) or `git rebase --continue`. `git merge --abort` returns to before the merge.

Conflicts are not errors; they are Git refusing to guess. Read both sides and understand why each changed.
lessons.analogy: A conflict is two editors changing the same sentence in a shared document. The software won't pick a winner; it highlights both versions and waits for the editor-in-chief (you).

example.code:
$ cat .gitignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
db.sqlite3
$ git merge feature/slow-api
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.py
$ git status --short
UU config.py
# edit config.py, keep timeout = 60, remove markers
$ git add config.py && git commit --no-edit
example.explain: `UU` = unmerged, both modified. After editing, `add` marks it resolved and the commit completes the merge.

terms: Patterns for files Git should not track.
Stop tracking a file but keep it on disk.
remember: Add `.env` to .gitignore before your first commit.
Leaked secret → rotate it; deleting it later isn't enough.
mistakes: Thinking a later commit removes a leaked secret from history.
Resolving by blindly choosing 'mine' without reading the other change.
interview: How do you stop tracking a file that's already committed?
Walk through resolving a merge conflict.
